title: International Union of Soil Sciences

definition.text: The international scientific union of soil scientists, founded in 1924 as the International Society of Soil Science and a member of the International Science Council.

facts.text: Its purpose is to promote all branches of soil science and their applications, foster contacts among soil scientists, and stimulate research and its use.
It has 86 national and regional member societies with about 60,000 scientists, plus individual members in 57 countries.
Every four years it holds the World Congress of Soil Science; after its founding meeting in Rome in 1924, the first congress met in Washington, D.C., in 1927.
Its commissions, grown from six set up in 1924, range from soil morphology and soil fertility to degradation control, soil education and the history of soil science.
Since 2014 the IUSS Council has elected its President for a two-year term; before that, the national society hosting the next World Congress designated the President.
It endorses the World Reference Base as the international standard for soil classification.
It publishes the monthly IUSS Alert and the twice-yearly IUSS Bulletin, and is a founding partner of the International Year of Planet Earth.
Since January 2023 its secretariat has been run by Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics.

notes: Albert Atterberg's article says the International Society of Soil Science recognized his classification at a 1913 Berlin conference (S:f454d8d8ec5a), eleven years before the society's 1924 founding; probably a predecessor conference. The four-yearly congress sentence (S:77bd0c3230c3) is tagged citation needed.

title: Soil Science Society of America

definition.text: The largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States, formed in 1936.

facts.text: It was formed in 1936 by merging the Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy with the American Soil Survey Association.
The ASA Soils Section became the official Americas section of the International Union of Soil Sciences in 1934, a role the society still fills.
Based in Madison, Wisconsin, it publishes peer-reviewed journals, magazines and books, led by its official Soil Science Society of America Journal.
Its voluntary certifications set standards for Certified Professional Soil Scientists and Certified Professional Soil Classifiers.
In 2011 it named soil science's grand challenges: climate change, food and energy security, waste treatment and water quality, and human and ecosystem health.
In 2017 it updated its definition of soil to cover loose material shaped by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near any planetary surface.
Its outreach includes the 'Secrets of Soil' exhibition, first shown at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History, and the school websites Soils4Teachers and soils4kids.
Past presidents include William Albrecht in 1939, Hans Jenny in 1949 and Rattan Lal in 2007.

title: International Soil Reference and Information Centre
article: International Soil Reference and Information Centre

definition.text: ISRIC, an independent, science-based foundation that provides quality-assessed soil information to address global environmental and societal challenges.

facts.text: It was established in 1966 on the recommendation of the International Society of Soil Science, now the IUSS, and UNESCO.
It works to widen the use of quality-assessed soil data, developing soil information standards, harmonised global soil products and stronger national and regional soil information systems.
Since 1989 it has been accredited as the World Data Centre for Soils, and its flagship products are the World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) and SoilGrids.
It houses the World Soil Museum and the World Soil Reference Collection, and ISRIC's Otto Spaargaren was nominated to help draft the World Reference Base.

title: Natural Resources Conservation Service

definition.text: An agency of the United States Department of Agriculture, formerly the Soil Conservation Service, that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners and managers.

facts.text: It began as the Soil Erosion Service, formed in the Department of the Interior on September 13, 1933, with Hugh Hammond Bennett as chief.
Bennett, driven by his knowledge of the soil erosion behind the 1930s Dust Bowl, led the founding and remained chief until he retired in 1952.
Moved to the Department of Agriculture on March 23, 1935, it was soon combined with other USDA units to form the Soil Conservation Service.
The SCS ran 500 Civilian Conservation Corps camps between 1933 and 1942, mainly for erosion control, and promoted practices such as contour plowing.
It was renamed the Natural Resources Conservation Service in 1994 to reflect its broader mission.
It gives farmers and ranchers technical and financial help, the money authorized by the Farm Bill, which is renewed every five years.
It leads the federal soil survey through the National Cooperative Soil Survey, with products such as the Web Soil Survey and the SSURGO database.
In 2015 it began broad support of soil health, promoting less tillage and more cover crops to reduce erosion and improve soil diversity.

conflicts.text: The agency currently has about 12,000 employees.
conflicts.note: The article's infobox gives approximately 11,000 employees (S:ff6285d91520).

notes: S:5e81bd34b4d5 names the 'Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1935' but links the Act of 1936; the Dust Bowl article says the agency was renamed the Soil Conservation Service in 1935 (S:2da445d82ee0). Worth checking the act's name and year.

definition.text: A nationwide US partnership of federal, regional, state and local agencies and institutions that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets the nation's soils and publishes the results.

facts.text: Led by the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service, it joins federal land agencies, state agricultural experiment stations, counties and conservation districts.
It inventories soils to judge land capability and conservation needs, and supplies soil information to the public, mainly through maps.
More than 90% of private lands have been mapped; in FY2001 maps were made or updated for 21,900,000 acres.
Federal authority for the soil survey comes from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896, and the survey has involved several partners since its inception that year.
Survey work moved among USDA units, from an 1894 Division of Agricultural Soil to the Bureau of Soils in 1901, before passing to the Soil Conservation Service in 1952.
Land-grant universities have been close partners from the start, and conservation districts and Cooperative Extension are partners today.
Soil series established through the NCSS form a level of the USDA Soil Taxonomy hierarchy.
The first surveys cost about 3/10ths of a cent per acre; by 1999 a survey cost about $3 an acre.

title: Early United States soil survey

definition.text: The beginnings of systematic soil survey in the United States, from the first field mapping in 1899 to the consolidation of all USDA survey work in 1952.

facts.text: Milton Whitney began field work on May 3, 1899, with $16,000, mapping about 720,000 acres that year in tobacco lands and alkali areas slated for irrigation.

The first surveyors, geologists or chemists without agronomy training, separated soils mainly by texture, later adding colour, organic content, structure and drainage, and grouped soil types into series.
Influenced by Hilgard, Hopkins and Glinka's Russian school, Curtis Marbut, in charge from 1913, came to treat soil science as distinct from geology and to describe soils by horizons.
From 1933 to 1952 the Soil Conservation Service clashed with the Bureau of Chemistry and Soils over survey methods, until all USDA soil survey work was consolidated under the SCS.

notes: The section also covers Marbut's pedocal/pedalfer scheme and the approximations leading to USDA soil taxonomy (1975, 1999), left to the classification chapter, and the 1951 Land Capability System (S:803e3f873d69).

definition.text: One of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, and formerly the Rothamsted Experimental Station.

facts.text: John Bennet Lawes, who had founded one of the first artificial fertilizer factories in 1842, set it up on his Rothamsted Manor estate to study how fertilizers affect crop yields.
With Joseph Henry Gilbert, who had trained under Liebig, Lawes began long-term field experiments; over 57 years they laid the foundations of scientific agriculture and crop nutrition.
The Broadbalk Experiment has been sown with winter wheat every year since 1843, and the Park Grass Experiment has been monitored continuously since 1856.
Thomas Way and Lawes discovered the principle of cation exchange there in the 19th century.
Its research led to single superphosphate fertilizer in the mid-nineteenth century, and in 1878 Robert Warington confirmed soil nitrification there.
In 1919 Ronald Fisher was hired to analyse its accumulated field data and stayed to create the theory of experimental design.
E. John Russell directed it from 1912 to 1943 and William Gammie Ogg until 1958, as staff grew from 140 to 471 and new departments, including pedology, were created.
Merged into the Institute of Arable Crops Research in 1987, it now operates as Rothamsted Research, funded mainly through the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

definition.text: A network of national soil science institutions, created in 1996 at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra, that collects and harmonises soil information for Europe.

facts.text: Staff of the JRC's Land Management Unit run it, hosting the network's secretariat and providing a central source of soil information for the European Commission.
It is organised as a network of 'Centres of Excellence'.
Demand for its information is rising to tackle agrochemical leaching, heavy metals, waste disposal, loss of soil structure, erosion and other environmental problems.

definition.text: A scientific society devoted to research on natural organic matter in soil and water.

facts.text: It was founded in Denver, Colorado, on September 11, 1981, to bring together coal, soil and water scientists interested in humic substances.
As of 2023 it had about 450 members in 24 country and regional chapters.
It keeps standard and reference samples of humic and fulvic acids from leonardite, river water, a mineral soil and peat, used by scientists in about 40 countries.
It advocates standard laboratory methods for preparing humic and fulvic acids and holds biennial international conferences.

definition.text: ICOMANTH, a committee active from 1995 to 2013 that worked on classifying soils derived from human activity.

facts.text: According to the NRCS, its main contribution was improving technical standards for describing anthropogenic soils and defining the taxa to classify them.
Ray Bryant chaired it at its founding and was succeeded by John Galbraith in 2004.
The NRCS judged its task complete, and several of its proposed changes were added to the soil taxonomy in 2014.

title: Soil Science Society of Poland

definition.text: The scientific and professional society of Polish soil scientists (Polskie Towarzystwo Gleboznawcze).

facts.text: It was founded in 1937 on the initiative of Feliks Terlikowski, Jan Włodek and Tadeusz Mieczyński.
It promotes soil science, pedology, agricultural chemistry and agricultural microbiology in Poland; in 2017 it had about 450 members in 14 regional and 4 thematic divisions.
A member of the IUSS, it publishes the journal Soil Science Annual, founded in 1950 as Roczniki Gleboznawcze.
It initiates and publishes the Polish Soil Classification, whose 5th edition appeared in 2011 and 6th in 2019.

title: Soil Science Society of America Journal
article: Soil Science Society of America Journal

definition.text: A bimonthly peer-reviewed journal publishing research on all aspects of soil science.

facts.text: It began in 1937 as Soil Science Society of America Proceedings, with J. D. Luckett as founding editor, and took its present title in 1973.
It is the flagship journal of the Soil Science Society of America.
Since 2013 it has been published only online, and its articles undergo double-blind review.
